definition: A logic gate whose output is 1 only when every input is 1.
wrongs: A gate whose output is 1 when at least one input is 1.
A gate whose output is the opposite of its single input.
A gate whose output is 1 only when its two inputs differ.
why: The AND operation is 1 only for the input combination in which all inputs are 1.
example: A lab safe opens only when the key switch and the PIN switch are both closed.
scenario: A two-input gate receives 1 and 0. Its output is 1 only if both inputs are 1. State the output.
scenarioWhy: Because one input is 0, an AND of 1 and 0 is 0.

definition: A logic gate whose output is 1 when at least one input is 1.
wrongs: A gate whose output is 1 only when every input is 1.
A gate whose output is 0 when any input is 1.
A gate whose output copies the complement of one input.
why: OR is 0 only when every input is 0, so any 1 forces the output to 1.
example: A hallway lamp lights if either the north switch or the south switch is closed.
scenario: A two-input gate outputs 1 when either input is 1. Both inputs are 0. State the output.
scenarioWhy: OR is 1 only when at least one input is 1, so two zeros produce 0.

definition: A one-input gate whose output is the complement of its input.
wrongs: A gate that outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1.
A gate that outputs 1 when the inputs differ.
A gate that stores one bit on a clock edge.
why: Negation swaps 0 and 1, which is the inverter function.
example: An alarm lamp is dark while a sensor wire is high, and it lights when that wire goes low.
scenario: An inverter receives a 1 on its only input. State the output.
scenarioWhy: An inverter complements its input, so an input of 1 produces 0.

definition: A gate that performs AND and then complements the result, so the output is 0 only when every input is 1.
wrongs: A gate that outputs 1 only when every input is 1.
A gate that outputs 1 only when every input is 0.
A gate that outputs 1 only when the inputs differ.
why: NAND is the complement of AND, so the all-ones input is the only case with output 0.
example: A warning LED stays lit unless two enable switches are both on, in which case the LED goes dark.
scenario: A two-input NAND gate receives 1 and 1. State the output.
scenarioWhy: NAND of 1 and 1 is the complement of 1, which is 0.

definition: A gate that performs OR and then complements the result, so the output is 1 only when every input is 0.
wrongs: A gate that outputs 1 when at least one input is 1.
A gate that outputs 0 only when every input is 1.
A gate that outputs 1 when the inputs are equal.
why: NOR is the complement of OR, so only the all-zero input produces a 1.
example: A green ready lamp lights only when both fault sensors are inactive.
scenario: A two-input NOR gate receives 0 and 0. State the output.
scenarioWhy: NOR is 1 only when every input is 0.

definition: A two-input gate whose output is 1 only when the inputs differ.
wrongs: A two-input gate whose output is 1 only when the inputs are the same.
A gate whose output is 1 only when both inputs are 1.
A gate whose output is 1 only when both inputs are 0.
why: Exclusive OR excludes the case where both inputs are 1, so it is true only for differing inputs.
example: A comparator lamp lights when two sensor bits disagree and stays dark when they match.
scenario: A two-input XOR gate receives 1 and 1. State the output.
scenarioWhy: XOR is 1 only when the inputs differ, and 1 with 1 is not a difference.

definition: A two-input gate whose output is 1 only when the inputs are the same.
wrongs: A two-input gate whose output is 1 only when the inputs differ.
A gate whose output is 1 when at least one input is 1.
A one-input gate that complements its input.
why: XNOR is the complement of XOR, so matching inputs produce 1.
example: An equality lamp lights only when two one-bit flags have the same value.
scenario: A two-input XNOR gate receives 1 and 0. State the output.
scenarioWhy: XNOR is 1 only when both inputs match, and 1 and 0 do not match.

definition: A gate type, such as NAND or NOR, from which any Boolean function can be built.
wrongs: A gate type that can build only AND functions.
A gate type that can build only XOR functions.
A memory element that stores one bit.
why: NAND alone, and NOR alone, can implement NOT, AND, and OR, and therefore any Boolean function.
example: A lab stocked only with NAND chips still builds an inverter, an AND, and a full adder.
scenario: A lab has only NAND chips. Can every Boolean function still be built?
scenarioWhy: NAND is universal, so every Boolean function can be built from NAND chips alone.

definition: A table that lists every input combination of a logic function and the output for each combination.
wrongs: A grid that groups adjacent 1s to simplify an expression.
A plot of signals against time.
A binary code in which neighbors differ by one bit.
why: Two inputs have four rows, and each row states the output for that combination.
example: A sheet lists 00, 01, 10, and 11, and beside 11 it records an output of 1 for a two-input AND.
scenario: A designer lists all four input pairs of a two-input function and writes the output beside each pair. Name that listing.
scenarioWrongs: A plot of signals versus time
A code whose neighbors differ by one bit
scenarioWhy: Listing every input combination with its output is a truth table.

definition: The algebra of the values 0 and 1 using AND, OR, and NOT, together with laws for simplifying expressions.
wrongs: The algebra of real numbers using addition and multiplication only.
A table of voltages versus time for an analog filter.
A method that solves circuits with mesh currents.
why: Switching functions obey identities such as idempotent, complement, and distributive laws on 0 and 1.
example: A designer replaces A OR (A AND B) with A by applying an absorption identity before drawing the gates.
scenario: A designer simplifies A + A·B to A using switching identities on 0 and 1. Name that algebra.
scenarioAnswer: The algebra of 0 and 1 with AND, OR, and NOT
scenarioWhy: Identities that simplify expressions in AND, OR, and NOT belong to Boolean algebra.

definition: The pair of identities that a complemented AND equals the OR of complements, and a complemented OR equals the AND of complements.
wrongs: The claim that AND and OR are the same operation.
The rule that a K-map group must contain six cells.
The rule that a flip-flop samples data only while the clock is low for the whole pulse.
why: Breaking a bubble on an AND or OR gate swaps the operation and complements the inputs.
example: A designer replaces a bubbled AND, with inputs already complemented, by a plain OR of those complemented inputs.
scenario: A circuit needs the complement of A AND B. Which expression is equal to it?
scenarioWhy: De Morgan's law says the complement of a product is the sum of the complements.

definition: A Boolean form written as an OR of AND terms.
wrongs: A Boolean form written as an AND of OR terms.
A sequential circuit that stores state in flip-flops.
A counter whose stages share one clock.
why: Each product term is an AND, and the function ORs those terms together.
example: The expression A·B + A·C is drawn as two AND gates feeding one OR gate.
scenario: An expression is written as A·B + C·D. Which form is that?
scenarioWrongs: A counter with one shared clock
scenarioWhy: A·B and C·D are products, and the plus sign ORs them, so the form is a sum of products.

definition: A Boolean form written as an AND of OR terms.
wrongs: A Boolean form written as an OR of AND terms.
A code in which successive values differ by one bit.
A gate output that can disconnect into high impedance.
why: Each sum term is an OR, and the function ANDs those terms together.
example: The expression (A + B)·(C + D) is drawn as two OR gates feeding one AND gate.
scenario: An expression is written as (A + B)·(C + D). Which form is that?
scenarioWhy: (A + B) and (C + D) are sums, and they are multiplied, so the form is a product of sums.

definition: A grid that simplifies a Boolean function by grouping adjacent cells of 1s or don't-cares in powers of two.
wrongs: A listing of signals plotted against time.
A bistable circuit that stores one bit.
A programmable array used only as a memory chip.
why: Neighboring cells differ by one variable, so a power-of-two group eliminates the changing variables.
example: On a 4-variable grid, a designer circles a block of four adjacent 1s and drops two literals from that term.
scenario: Adjacent cells of a simplification grid differ by how many input bits?
scenarioWhy: Karnaugh-map neighbors are placed so they differ by exactly one bit.

definition: An input combination whose output may be treated as either 0 or 1 because it never occurs or does not matter.
wrongs: An input combination that must always produce 0.
An input combination that must always produce 1.
A timing pulse that clocks every flip-flop.
why: Unused combinations can be assigned whichever value makes larger simplification groups.
example: A BCD function never receives the codes 1010 through 1111, so those cells may be circled or ignored.
scenario: Codes 1010 through 1111 never occur in a BCD function. How may their outputs be treated during simplification?
scenarioWhy: Combinations that never occur are don't-cares, so either output value is allowed.

definition: A logic circuit whose outputs depend only on the present inputs and not on stored state.
wrongs: A circuit whose outputs depend on stored state as well as the inputs.
A counter built from clocked flip-flops.
A register that shifts bits on each clock.
why: With no memory elements, the same inputs always produce the same outputs.
example: A decoder built only from gates drives one of eight lamps, and the lamps depend only on the three input bits right now.
scenario: A gate network has no feedback and no stored bits, so the same inputs always give the same outputs. Which class of circuit is it?
scenarioAnswer: Output depends only on present inputs
scenarioWhy: No memory means the outputs are a function of the present inputs alone.

definition: A logic circuit whose outputs depend on the present inputs and on state stored in memory elements.
wrongs: A circuit whose outputs depend only on the present inputs.
A gate network with no feedback and no storage.
A truth table with no clock.
why: Flip-flops or latches remember prior inputs, so the output can differ for the same present input.
example: A turnstile controller stays locked or unlocked according to coins already inserted, not only the button pressed now.
scenario: A controller gives different outputs for the same button press because it remembers earlier coins. Which class of circuit is it?
scenarioWrongs: Output depends only on present inputs
scenarioWhy: Remembering earlier inputs means the circuit is sequential.

definition: A combinational circuit that adds two bits and produces a sum and a carry, with no carry input.
wrongs: A circuit that adds two bits plus a carry input.
A circuit that selects one of many data inputs.
A circuit that stores an eight-bit word.
why: The sum is the XOR of the two bits, and the carry is their AND.
example: Adding the bits 1 and 1 in a two-input adder block yields sum 0 and carry 1.
scenario: A block adds the bits 1 and 1 and has no carry input. State the sum and carry as sum,carry.
scenarioWhy: 1 plus 1 is 0 with a carry of 1, which is what a half adder produces.

definition: A combinational circuit that adds two bits and a carry-in, and produces a sum and a carry-out.
wrongs: A circuit that adds two bits and has no carry input.
A circuit that only compares two numbers.
A circuit that routes one input to many outputs.
why: The sum is the XOR of the three inputs, and the carry-out is the majority function of those inputs.
example: Adding 1, 1, and a carry-in of 1 in a three-input adder yields sum 1 and carry-out 1.
scenario: A block adds bits 1 and 1 together with a carry-in of 1. State the sum and carry-out as sum,carry.
scenarioWhy: 1 + 1 + 1 equals 3, which is sum 1 and carry-out 1.

definition: A combinational circuit that forwards one of several data inputs to a single output, chosen by select lines.
wrongs: A circuit that routes one data input to one of several outputs.
A circuit that turns a binary code into one active line.
A circuit that turns one active line into a binary code.
why: The select inputs choose which data input is connected to the output.
example: A four-input data selector uses two select switches to pass exactly one of four sensor signals onward.
scenario: A data selector has four data inputs. How many select lines does it need?
scenarioWhy: Four inputs require two select bits because 2 to the power 2 is 4.

definition: A combinational circuit that routes one data input to one of several outputs, chosen by select lines.
wrongs: A circuit that forwards one of several data inputs to a single output.
A circuit that adds three bits.
A circuit that stores a bit on a clock edge.
why: The select inputs choose which output receives the single data input.
example: One serial data wire is steered to exactly one of eight lamps by three address switches.
scenario: One data wire must be steered to exactly one of eight outputs. How many select lines are required?
scenarioWhy: Eight outputs require three select bits because 2 to the power 3 is 8.

definition: A combinational circuit that converts one active input line into the binary number of that line.
wrongs: A circuit that converts a binary code into one active output line.
A circuit that adds a carry-in to two data bits.
A circuit that compares two unsigned numbers.
why: If input line k is the active line, the encoder outputs the binary representation of k.
example: When only input line 5 of an 8-line encoder is active, the outputs show the binary value 101.
scenario: Only input line 5 is active on an 8-to-3 encoder. State the 3-bit output.
scenarioWhy: Decimal 5 is binary 101, so the encoder outputs 101.

definition: A combinational circuit that converts a binary code into one active output line.
wrongs: A circuit that converts one active input line into a binary code.
A circuit that selects one of several data inputs.
A shift register that moves bits each clock.
why: An n-bit code can activate one of up to 2 to the power n output lines.
example: The code 011 on a 3-to-8 decoder makes output line 3 active and leaves the other seven inactive.
scenario: A 3-to-8 decoder receives the code 011. Which output line becomes active, numbering lines from 0?
scenarioWhy: Binary 011 is decimal 3, so output line 3 is the active line.

definition: A combinational circuit that compares two binary numbers and reports which is larger or that they are equal.
wrongs: A circuit that adds two bits and a carry-in.
A circuit that stores one bit and toggles when T is 1.
A circuit that generates an even parity bit only.
why: The outputs indicate the three relations greater-than, equal, and less-than.
example: Comparing 1010 with 1001 raises the greater-than output and leaves equal and less-than inactive.
scenario: A comparator receives A = 1010 and B = 1001. Which relation output is active?
scenarioWhy: Binary 1010 is decimal 10 and 1001 is decimal 9, so A is greater.

definition: A bistable circuit that stores one bit and is set or reset by two inputs, with both inputs active disallowed.
wrongs: An edge-triggered element that copies D to Q on the clock edge.
A gate network with no storage.
A counter that cycles through ten states.
why: Cross-coupled NOR or NAND gates hold a bit until a set or reset input changes it.
example: Pressing Set makes a NOR latch output stay 1 after the button is released, until Reset is pressed.
scenario: A NOR latch has S = 1 and R = 0. What happens to Q?
scenarioWhy: For a NOR SR latch, S = 1 and R = 0 sets Q to 1.

definition: An edge-triggered element that copies its D input to Q on the active clock edge.
wrongs: A level-sensitive latch that is set or reset by two inputs.
An element that toggles when both J and K are 1.
A gate that outputs the AND of its inputs.
why: The data input is sampled at the clock edge and then held until the next active edge.
example: On the rising clock edge, a register bit changes from 0 to 1 because its D pin was 1 just before that edge.
scenario: Just before the active clock edge, D is 1 and Q is 0. Immediately after that edge, what is Q?
scenarioWhy: A D flip-flop copies D to Q on the active clock edge.

definition: A bistable element that can set, reset, hold, or toggle, and that toggles when J and K are both active.
wrongs: An element that only copies D to Q and cannot toggle.
A memoryless gate with no clock.
A decoder with eight outputs.
why: J = 1 and K = 0 sets the flip-flop, J = 0 and K = 1 resets it, and J = K = 1 toggles it.
example: With J and K both held at 1, the stored bit flips on every active clock edge.
scenario: J and K are both 1 at an active clock edge. What does the flip-flop do?
scenarioWrongs: It clears Q and stays cleared
scenarioWhy: J = K = 1 is the toggle condition of a JK flip-flop.

definition: A clocked bistable element that toggles its stored bit when T is active and holds it when T is inactive.
wrongs: An element that copies a data input and never toggles on its own.
A latch with separate set and reset inputs.
A combinational adder with no clock.
why: T stands for toggle: an active T changes Q on the clock event, and an inactive T leaves Q unchanged.
example: A divide-by-two stage uses a toggle flip-flop with T tied to 1, so Q flips on every clock.
scenario: T is tied to 1. How does Q change on the next active clock edge?
scenarioWhy: With T held active, a T flip-flop toggles on each active clock edge.

definition: Sampling of a flip-flop input only during a clock transition, not during the whole time the clock is active.
wrongs: Sampling that continues for the entire time the clock level is high.
A delay measured from an input change to a valid output.
A requirement that data stay stable after the clock edge.
why: A rising-edge or falling-edge device ignores the data input except at that transition.
example: Data may chatter while the clock is high, but a rising-edge flip-flop changes only at the upward crossing.
scenario: A flip-flop ignores D while the clock is high and samples D only on the rising crossing. Name that sampling style.
scenarioWrongs: Sampling during the whole high level
A delay until the output is valid
scenarioWhy: Sampling only at the rising crossing is edge triggering.

definition: The minimum time that data must be stable before the active clock edge for reliable capture.
wrongs: The minimum time that data must remain stable after the active clock edge.
The delay from a gate input change until the output is valid.
The high time of a periodic clock waveform.
why: The internal sampling nodes of a flip-flop need the data to be valid before the clock arrives.
example: A datasheet requires D to be steady for 5 ns before the rising clock, or the captured bit may be wrong.
scenario: A datasheet says D must be stable for 5 ns before the rising clock. Name that 5 ns requirement.
scenarioWrongs: Delay until the output is valid
scenarioWhy: Time that data must be stable before the active edge is setup time.

definition: The minimum time that data must remain stable after the active clock edge for reliable capture.
wrongs: The minimum time that data must be stable before the active clock edge.
The number of gate inputs one output can drive.
The number of states in a counter cycle.
why: After the clock edge, the flip-flop still needs a short interval before D is allowed to change.
example: A datasheet requires D to stay unchanged for 2 ns after the rising edge, even if the next value is already available.
scenario: A datasheet says D must remain stable for 2 ns after the rising clock. Name that 2 ns requirement.
scenarioWrongs: How many inputs one output can drive
How many states a counter has
scenarioWhy: Time that data must stay stable after the active edge is hold time.

definition: The time from an input change until the corresponding output becomes valid.
wrongs: The time data must be stable before a clock edge.
The time data must remain stable after a clock edge.
The period of the system clock.
why: Gates and flip-flops cannot respond instantly, so the output lags the input by a specified delay.
example: A gate input switches at time zero, and the output crosses its valid level 8 ns later.
scenario: A gate input changes, and the output becomes valid 8 ns later. What is that 8 ns interval called?
scenarioWhy: The lag from an input change to a valid output is propagation delay.

definition: A group of flip-flops that stores a multi-bit value and shares a common clock.
wrongs: A single gate that computes AND.
A memoryless decoder.
A truth table written on paper.
why: Each flip-flop holds one bit, so n flip-flops hold an n-bit word.
example: Eight rising-edge flip-flops share one clock and together hold the value loaded from eight data pins.
scenario: Eight flip-flops share one clock and together hold one loaded word. Name that structure.
scenarioWhy: Clocked flip-flops that store a word form a register.

definition: A register that moves its stored bits one position to the left or the right on each clock.
wrongs: A register that only loads all bits in parallel and never moves them.
A combinational circuit that adds two bits.
A gate with a high-impedance output state.
why: Each clock moves every bit into the neighboring flip-flop, which builds serial-to-parallel conversion.
example: A four-bit serial input 1101 enters one pin, and after four clocks the four flip-flops hold 1101.
scenario: Bits enter one pin, and each clock moves every stored bit one position toward the next flip-flop. Name that register.
scenarioAnswer: A register that moves bits each clock
scenarioWrongs: A register that never moves bits
scenarioWhy: Moving stored bits one position per clock is the behavior of a shift register.

definition: An asynchronous counter in which each flip-flop is clocked by the output of the previous stage.
wrongs: A counter in which every flip-flop receives the same clock.
A register that does not count.
A combinational comparator.
why: The clock ripples from stage to stage, so the outputs do not all change at the same instant.
example: In a 3-bit up counter, the first flip-flop's output clocks the second, and the second clocks the third.
scenario: In a counter, flip-flop 1 is clocked by the output of flip-flop 0 rather than by the system clock. Which counter style is that?
scenarioAnswer: Clock ripples from stage to stage
scenarioWrongs: A register that does not count
scenarioWhy: Clocking each stage from the previous output is a ripple counter.

definition: A counter in which every flip-flop receives the same clock, so state bits change together.
wrongs: A counter whose clock ripples from one stage to the next.
A latch with no clock at all.
A gate delay called a hazard.
why: A common clock removes the accumulated ripple delay between stages.
example: All three flip-flops of a binary up counter share one clock pin, and combinational logic forms the next state.
scenario: All flip-flops of a counter share one clock pin, and logic computes the next state. Which counter style is that?
scenarioWhy: A shared clock for every stage makes the counter synchronous.

definition: A counter that returns to its starting state after a fixed number of distinct states.
wrongs: A register that only shifts and never returns to a count.
A decoder with a fixed number of outputs but no state.
A gate whose delay is fixed.
why: A modulo-n counter has n states, so a decade counter has modulus 10.
example: A decade counter visits ten states, 0 through 9, and then returns to 0.
scenario: A counter visits the states 0 through 9 and then returns to 0. State its modulus.
scenarioWhy: Ten distinct states mean the modulus is 10.

definition: A bipolar-transistor logic family, typified by the 74xx series, that uses a multi-emitter transistor input.
wrongs: A logic family built from complementary n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs.
A current-steering family known for very small voltage swings.
A historical family that used only resistors and diodes at the input.
why: Classic transistor-transistor logic uses bipolar transistors and a multi-emitter input stage.
example: A 7400 package contains four bipolar NAND gates and is powered near 5 V.
scenario: A 7400 chip uses bipolar transistors and a multi-emitter input for its NAND gates. Name that logic family.
scenarioWhy: The 74xx bipolar family with a multi-emitter input is TTL.

definition: A logic family that uses complementary n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs and draws almost no static current.
wrongs: A bipolar family typified by the 7400 NAND gate.
A diode-only logic family with no transistors.
A vacuum-tube logic family.
why: In a static CMOS gate, one of the complementary networks is off, so almost no current flows from supply to ground.
example: A battery-powered door lock uses complementary MOSFET gates so the idle circuit draws almost no current.
scenario: A gate uses paired n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs and draws almost no current while idle. Name that family.
scenarioWhy: Complementary n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs with almost no static current identify CMOS.

definition: The largest number of similar gate inputs that one output can drive while meeting its voltage specifications.
wrongs: The noise voltage a gate can tolerate.
The delay from input to output.
The number of states in a counter.
why: Each added input draws current or capacitance, and too many inputs pull the output out of its valid voltage range.
example: A datasheet allows one output to drive ten inputs of the same family, and an eleventh input would violate the voltage levels.
scenario: One output may drive at most ten inputs of the same family before voltage levels fail. Which limit is ten?
scenarioAnswer: How many inputs one output can drive
scenarioWrongs: How much noise voltage is allowed
scenarioWhy: The maximum number of similar inputs one output can drive is the fan-out.

definition: The largest noise voltage that can be added to a valid logic level and still be interpreted correctly.
wrongs: The number of inputs one gate output can drive.
The clock frequency of a counter.
The number of cells in a K-map group.
why: The gap between a guaranteed output level and the required input threshold is the noise margin.
example: A gate's lowest valid high output is 4.4 V and the next gate accepts a high above 3.5 V, leaving 0.9 V of margin.
scenario: The lowest valid high output is 4.4 V, and the next input treats a high as valid above 3.5 V. How much high-side noise margin, in volts, is there?
scenarioWhy: Noise margin is the difference 4.4 V minus 3.5 V, which is 0.9 V.

definition: A periodic waveform that tells sequential elements when to sample their inputs.
wrongs: A one-time power-on reset pulse.
A data bit stored in a register.
A don't-care entry in a truth table.
why: Edge-triggered flip-flops change state in step with the active edge of this waveform.
example: A square wave at 10 MHz is wired to every flip-flop clock pin on a counter board.
scenario: A 10 MHz square wave is wired to every flip-flop clock pin so they sample together. Name that waveform's role.
scenarioAnswer: It times when state is sampled
scenarioWrongs: It is a stored data bit
It is an unused truth-table entry
scenarioWhy: A periodic waveform that tells flip-flops when to sample is the clock.

definition: A momentary false pulse on an output that should have stayed constant when a single input changes.
wrongs: A repeated toggle of a level-sensitive JK while its clock stays high.
A missing power connection.
A correct change from 0 to 1 that is meant to happen.
why: Unequal gate delays can briefly break a covering term before another term turns on.
example: An output that should stay 1 glitches to 0 for a few nanoseconds when one input changes and two paths have different delays.
scenario: An output should stay 1, but unequal delays make it glitch to 0 for a few nanoseconds when one input changes. Name that fault.
scenarioWrongs: Repeated toggling while the clock is high
scenarioWhy: A brief incorrect pulse while the static output should be constant is a static hazard.

definition: Repeated toggling of a level-sensitive JK flip-flop while the clock stays active and both J and K are 1.
wrongs: A single brief glitch caused by unequal combinational delays.
A setup-time violation on an edge-triggered D flip-flop.
A don't-care used to enlarge a K-map group.
why: While the clock level remains enabling, the toggled output feeds back and toggles again if the pulse is longer than the delay.
example: A level-sensitive JK with J = K = 1 flips several times during one long clock-high pulse.
scenario: A level-sensitive JK has J = K = 1, and the clock stays high much longer than the flip-flop delay. What can Q do during that pulse?
scenarioWrongs: Become a don't-care in a map
scenarioWhy: A long enabling clock with J = K = 1 lets a level-sensitive JK toggle repeatedly, which is race-around.

definition: A binary code in which two successive values differ in exactly one bit.
wrongs: A code in which successive values may change many bits, such as ordinary binary.
A 7-bit code for English letters.
A parity scheme that adds one extra bit.
why: Changing only one bit between counts avoids false intermediate codes on mechanical or asynchronous sensors.
example: A rotary encoder moves from 01 to 11, changing only the higher bit, as the shaft turns to the next angle.
scenario: In 2-bit reflected Gray code, which code immediately follows 01?
scenarioWhy: The 2-bit Gray sequence is 00, 01, 11, 10, so 01 is followed by 11.

definition: An extra bit added so the total number of 1s in a group is even, or odd, in order to detect errors.
wrongs: A bit that corrects every possible multi-bit error by itself.
A clock bit that synchronizes flip-flops.
A sign bit in a two's-complement integer.
why: A single flipped bit changes the parity, so the receiver can detect that one-bit error.
example: The data 1011 has three 1s, so an even-parity extra bit of 1 makes the total number of 1s even.
scenario: Data bits are 1011, which contain three 1s. State the even-parity extra bit.
scenarioWhy: Even parity needs an even number of 1s, so three data 1s require an extra 1.

definition: A device with a programmable AND array and a programmable OR array used to realize sum-of-products functions.
wrongs: A device with a programmable AND array and a fixed OR array.
A read-only memory whose address lines fully decode every minterm.
A field-programmable gate array made only of lookup tables and routing.
why: Both the product terms and the sums that use them can be programmed in a PLA.
example: A designer programs which inputs enter each AND term and which of those terms enter each OR output.
scenario: A chip lets the designer program both which AND terms exist and which of those terms feed each OR output. Name that device style.
scenarioWhy: Programmable product terms and programmable sums describe a PLA.

definition: A plot of digital signals against time that shows their order, duration, and delays.
wrongs: A truth table that has no time axis.
A Karnaugh map used for simplification.
A pin diagram of a chip package.
why: Designers read setup, hold, and propagation relationships from waveforms drawn versus time.
example: A lab sheet draws the clock, D, and Q, showing Q changing 3 ns after the rising clock edge.
scenario: A sheet draws clock, D, and Q as waveforms and shows Q changing a few nanoseconds after the rising edge. Name that drawing.
scenarioWhy: Waveforms of clock, D, and Q versus time form a timing diagram.

definition: An output that can drive 0, drive 1, or disconnect into a high-impedance state.
wrongs: An output that can drive only 0 or 1 and cannot disconnect.
An output that drives only analog voltages.
An output that stores four bits.
why: The high-impedance state lets several devices share a bus without fighting.
example: Two memory chips share a data bus, and only the selected chip drives the lines while the other disconnects.
scenario: Two chips share a data bus, and the unselected chip must release the wires. Which output state lets it release them?
scenarioWhy: High impedance disconnects the driver so another chip can use the bus.

definition: A variable that can take only the two logic values 0 and 1.
wrongs: A variable that can take any real number.
A variable that stores a 32-bit floating-point value.
A variable that must be a character from an alphabet.
why: Switching algebra assigns each variable one of two values, matching a digital signal.
example: In the expression A + B, the letter A stands for a signal that is either low or high.
scenario: In a switching expression, signal A may be low or high and no other value. What kind of variable is A?
scenarioWhy: A signal restricted to low or high is a Boolean variable.
